# `flak`

A fast, simple CLI for linting YAML files.

## Features

- Lints `.yml` and `.yaml` files
- Checks for syntax errors and common formatting issues
- Supports individual files, directories, and glob patterns
- Friendly CLI output
- Non-zero exit codes on failure for CI use

## Installation

### Homebrew

```bash
brew install flak
```

### npm

```bash
npm install -g flak
```

### From source

```bash
git clone https://github.com/example/flak.git
cd flak
make install
```

## Usage

```bash
flak [options] [path ...]
```

If no path is provided, `flak` lints the current directory recursively.

### Examples

Lint a single file:

```bash
flak config.yaml
```

Lint multiple files:

```bash
flak app.yaml ci.yml
```

Lint a directory:

```bash
flak ./configs
```

Lint using a glob:

```bash
flak "configs/**/*.yaml"
```

## Options

| Option | Description |
|---|---|
| `-c, --config <path>` | Path to configuration file |
| `-f, --format <type>` | Output format: `text`, `json` |
| `--fix` | Automatically fix supported formatting issues |
| `-q, --quiet` | Only print errors |
| `-w, --watch` | Watch files and re-lint on changes |
| `--stdin` | Read YAML content from standard input |
| `--no-color` | Disable colored output |
| `-h, --help` | Show help |
| `-v, --version` | Show version |

## Configuration

`flak` can be configured with a `.flak.yml` file:

```yaml
extends: default

rules:
  indentation:
    spaces: 2
  document-start: off
  trailing-spaces: error
  key-duplicates: error

ignore:
  - vendor/**
  - node_modules/**
  - dist/**
```

## Rules

Example built-in rules include:

- `indentation`
- `trailing-spaces`
- `key-duplicates`
- `document-start`
- `line-length`
- `truthy-values`

## Exit codes

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `0` | No linting errors |
| `1` | Linting errors found |
| `2` | Invalid CLI usage or configuration |
| `3` | Unexpected runtime error |

## CI example

### GitHub Actions

```yaml
name: lint-yaml

on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  flak:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Install flak
        run: npm install -g flak
      - name: Run flak
        run: flak .
```

## Stdin support

You can pipe YAML directly into `flak`:

```bash
cat config.yaml | flak --stdin
```

Or:

```bash
kubectl get configmap my-app -o yaml | flak --stdin
```

## Ignore patterns

By default, `flak` skips common generated and dependency directories such as:

- `node_modules/`
- `.git/`
- `dist/`
- `vendor/`

You can customize ignore patterns in `.flak.yml`.

## Development

Run tests:

```bash
make test
```

Run linting locally:

```bash
make lint
```

# paw

A small React component library with 12 UI primitives for building clean, consistent interfaces.

## Features

- Lightweight and composable
- Simple API
- React-first design
- Suitable for design systems and app UIs
- Includes 12 foundational primitives

## Components

`paw` includes the following primitives:

1. `Box`
2. `Text`
3. `Button`
4. `Input`
5. `Textarea`
6. `Checkbox`
7. `Radio`
8. `Switch`
9. `Select`
10. `Badge`
11. `Divider`
12. `Stack`

## Installation

```bash
npm install paw
```

or

```bash
yarn add paw
```

or

```bash
pnpm add paw
```

## Usage

```tsx
import {
  Box,
  Text,
  Button,
  Input,
  Stack,
  Badge,
} from "paw";

export function App() {
  return (
    <Box padding="16px">
      <Stack gap="12px">
        <Text size="lg" weight="bold">
          Hello from paw
        </Text>

        <Input placeholder="Enter your name" />

        <Button variant="primary">Submit</Button>

        <Badge tone="success">Ready</Badge>
      </Stack>
    </Box>
  );
}
```

## Components Overview

### Box

A generic layout container.

```tsx
<Box padding="16px" background="#fff" borderRadius="8px">
  Content
</Box>
```

### Text

Typography primitive for rendering text.

```tsx
<Text size="md" weight="medium" color="#333">
  Simple text
</Text>
```

### Button

Interactive button for actions.

```tsx
<Button variant="primary" onClick={() => alert("Clicked")}>
  Click me
</Button>
```

### Input

Single-line text input.

```tsx
<Input placeholder="Email address" />
```

### Textarea

Multi-line text input.

```tsx
<Textarea placeholder="Write a message..." rows={4} />
```

### Checkbox

Binary selection control.

```tsx
<Checkbox defaultChecked>
  Accept terms
</Checkbox>
```

### Radio

Single-choice selection control.

```tsx
<Radio name="plan" value="pro">
  Pro
</Radio>
```

### Switch

Toggle control for on/off state.

```tsx
<Switch defaultChecked />
```

### Select

Dropdown selection input.

```tsx
<Select defaultValue="cat">
  <option value="cat">Cat</option>
  <option value="dog">Dog</option>
</Select>
```

### Badge

Small status or label indicator.

```tsx
<Badge tone="info">Beta</Badge>
```

### Divider

Visual separator between content.

```tsx
<Divider />
```

### Stack

Vertical or horizontal layout helper.

```tsx
<Stack direction="vertical" gap="8px">
  <Button>Save</Button>
  <Button variant="secondary">Cancel</Button>
</Stack>
```

## Example

```tsx
import {
  Box,
  Stack,
  Text,
  Input,
  Textarea,
  Checkbox,
  Radio,
  Switch,
  Select,
  Badge,
  Divider,
  Button,
} from "paw";

export function ProfileForm() {
  return (
    <Box padding="24px" background="#fafafa" borderRadius="12px">
      <Stack gap="16px">
        <Text size="xl" weight="bold">Profile settings</Text>

        <Input placeholder="Full name" />
        <Textarea placeholder="Bio" rows={3} />

        <Checkbox>Show profile publicly</Checkbox>

        <Stack direction="horizontal" gap="12px">
          <Radio name="role" value="user">User</Radio>
          <Radio name="role" value="admin">Admin</Radio>
        </Stack>

        <Switch defaultChecked />

        <Select defaultValue="light">
          <option value="light">Light</option>
          <option value="dark">Dark</option>
        </Select>

        <Divider />

        <Stack direction="horizontal" gap="8px" align="center">
          <Badge tone="success">Saved</Badge>
          <Button variant="primary">Update</Button>
        </Stack>
      </Stack>
    </Box>
  );
}
```

## Styling

`paw` is designed to work with minimal setup. Depending on the library implementation, components may:

- Ship with default styles
- Support inline style props
- Expose `className` for custom styling
- Integrate with CSS Modules, Tailwind, or CSS-in-JS

Example:

```tsx
<Button className="my-button">Custom Button</Button>
```

## Accessibility

`paw` aims to provide accessible building blocks:

- Semantic HTML where possible
- Keyboard-friendly interactions
- Focus-visible support
- Label-friendly form controls
- ARIA attributes where appropriate

## TypeScript

`paw` works well with TypeScript and provides typed component props.

```tsx
import { Button } from "paw";

function SaveButton() {
  return <Button variant="primary">Save</Button>;
}
```

git clone https://github.com/your-org/paw.git
cd paw

npm run dev

# paw

A tiny React component library with 12 small UI primitives for building clean, accessible interfaces.

## Features

- Lightweight and composable
- Built for React
- Small set of reusable primitives
- Accessibility-friendly defaults
- Easy to style and extend

## Installation

```bash
npm install paw
```

or

```bash
yarn add paw
```

or

```bash
pnpm add paw
```

## Usage

```tsx
import {
  Box,
  Text,
  Button,
  Input,
  Stack,
  Card,
} from "paw";

export default function App() {
  return (
    <Card>
      <Stack gap="12">
        <Text>Hello from paw</Text>
        <Input placeholder="Type here..." />
        <Button>Click me</Button>
      </Stack>
    </Card>
  );
}
```

## Components

`paw` includes 12 small UI primitives:

1. `Box` – Generic layout container
2. `Text` – Typography primitive
3. `Button` – Interactive button element
4. `Input` – Single-line text input
5. `Textarea` – Multi-line text input
6. `Label` – Accessible form label
7. `Stack` – Vertical or horizontal spacing layout
8. `Inline` – Inline row layout with wrapping support
9. `Card` – Simple surface container
10. `Divider` – Visual separator
11. `Avatar` – User image or fallback
12. `Badge` – Small status or metadata label

## Example

```tsx
import {
  Avatar,
  Badge,
  Box,
  Button,
  Card,
  Divider,
  Inline,
  Label,
  Stack,
  Text,
  Textarea,
  Input,
} from "paw";

export function ProfileCard() {
  return (
    <Card>
      <Stack gap="16">
        <Inline gap="12" align="center">
          <Avatar src="/avatar.png" alt="Jane Doe" />
          <Box>
            <Text weight="medium">Jane Doe</Text>
            <Inline gap="8">
              <Badge>Pro</Badge>
              <Badge tone="success">Active</Badge>
            </Inline>
          </Box>
        </Inline>

        <Divider />

        <Stack gap="8">
          <Label htmlFor="message">Message</Label>
          <Textarea id="message" placeholder="Write something..." />
        </Stack>

        <Stack gap="8">
          <Label htmlFor="email">Email</Label>
          <Input id="email" type="email" placeholder="jane@example.com" />
        </Stack>

        <Button>Send</Button>
      </Stack>
    </Card>
  );
}
```

## API Overview

### `Box`
A low-level wrapper for layout and styling.

```tsx
<Box as="section">Content</Box>
```

### `Text`
Text and typography primitive.

```tsx
<Text size="2" weight="medium">Hello</Text>
```

### `Button`
A styled button with sensible defaults.

```tsx
<Button variant="primary">Save</Button>
```

### `Input`
Basic text input.

```tsx
<Input placeholder="Your name" />
```

### `Textarea`
Multi-line input field.

```tsx
<Textarea rows={4} />
```

### `Label`
Label for form controls.

```tsx
<Label htmlFor="name">Name</Label>
```

### `Stack`
Layout children vertically or horizontally with consistent gaps.

```tsx
<Stack gap="12">
  <Box>One</Box>
  <Box>Two</Box>
</Stack>
```

### `Inline`
Inline layout with spacing and wrapping.

```tsx
<Inline gap="8">
  <Badge>Design</Badge>
  <Badge>React</Badge>
</Inline>
```

### `Card`
Surface container for grouped content.

```tsx
<Card>
  <Text>Inside a card</Text>
</Card>
```

### `Divider`
Horizontal or vertical separator.

```tsx
<Divider />
```

### `Avatar`
Displays a profile image, initials, or fallback content.

```tsx
<Avatar src="/user.png" alt="User" />
```

### `Badge`
Compact label for status or categories.

```tsx
<Badge tone="neutral">New</Badge>
```

## Styling

`paw` is designed to work with your styling approach:

- Plain CSS
- CSS Modules
- Tailwind CSS
- Styled Components
- Emotion

Example:

```tsx
<Button className="my-button">Custom Button</Button>
```

## Accessibility

The primitives are designed with accessibility in mind:

- Semantic HTML where possible
- Form-friendly components
- Keyboard-accessible interactions
- Label/input pairing support
- Sensible focus behavior

## TypeScript

`paw` includes TypeScript types out of the box.

```tsx
import { Button } from "paw";

type Props = {
  onSubmit: () => void;
};

export function SaveButton({ onSubmit }: Props) {
  return <Button onClick={onSubmit}>Save</Button>;
}
```

## Contributing

Contributions, issues, and ideas are welcome.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/your-name/paw.git
cd paw
npm install
npm run dev
```

## Scripts

```bash
npm run build
npm run test
npm run lint
```

        </Inline>

      </Stack>

}

### Box

A low-level wrapper for layout and spacing.

```jsx
import { Box } from 'paw';

<Box padding="md" radius="md">
  Content
</Box>

### Text

Use for body copy, labels, and headings.

import { Text } from 'paw';

<Text size="lg" weight="semibold">

Trigger actions.

import { Button } from 'paw';

import { Input } from 'paw';

<Input placeholder="Type here..." />

<>

Container with surface styling.

</Stack>

  <Badge>New</Badge>

</Inline>

Separate content sections.

import { Divider } from 'paw';

<Divider />

Small label for status, category, or counts.

import { Badge } from 'paw';

  background: rebeccapurple;

# tiny-date

**tiny-date** is a tiny, dependency-free library for formatting dates relative to now.

Turn timestamps into human-friendly strings like:

- `just now`
- `5 minutes ago`
- `in 2 days`

## Features

- Small and simple
- No dependencies
- Works with `Date`, timestamps, and date strings
- Relative formatting for past and future dates

## Installation

```bash
npm install tiny-date
```

Or with yarn:

```bash
yarn add tiny-date
```

## Usage

```js
import { relativeDate } from "tiny-date";

relativeDate(new Date(Date.now() - 5 * 60 * 1000));
// "5 minutes ago"

relativeDate(new Date(Date.now() + 2 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000));
// "in 2 days"
```

### Common examples

```js
relativeDate(new Date()); // "just now"

relativeDate(Date.now() - 60 * 60 * 1000); // "1 hour ago"

relativeDate("2024-01-01T00:00:00Z"); // "X ago" or "in X" depending on current date
```

## API

### `relativeDate(date, [options])`

Returns a relative time string based on the current time.

#### Parameters

- `date`  
  A `Date`, timestamp, or parseable date string.

- `options` *(optional)*  
  Configuration object.

#### Options

- `now`  
  A custom reference time. Defaults to `Date.now()`.

- `style`  
  Formatting style:
  - `"long"`: `5 minutes ago`
  - `"short"`: `5 min ago`

#### Returns

A human-readable relative time string.

## Example with options

```js
import { relativeDate } from "tiny-date";

relativeDate(Date.now() - 90 * 1000, { style: "short" });
// "2 min ago"

relativeDate(Date.now() + 3 * 60 * 60 * 1000, { now: Date.now(), style: "long" });
// "in 3 hours"

Examples:

- `5 minutes ago`
- `in 2 days`
- `just now`
- `3 weeks ago`

## Features

- Tiny and fast
- No dependencies
- Human-readable relative time formatting
- Works with JavaScript `Date` objects, timestamps, and date-like values

## Installation

```bash
npm install tiny-date
```

or

```bash
yarn add tiny-date
```

## Usage

```js
import { formatRelative } from "tiny-date";

console.log(formatRelative(new Date(Date.now() - 5 * 60 * 1000)));
// "5 minutes ago"

console.log(formatRelative(new Date(Date.now() + 2 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000)));
// "in 2 days"
```

## API

### `formatRelative(date, [options])`

Formats a date relative to the current time.

#### Parameters

- `date`  
  A `Date`, timestamp, or other date-like value.

- `options` *(optional)*  
  An options object.

#### Options

- `now`  
  The reference time to compare against. Defaults to `Date.now()`.

- `justNowThreshold`  
  The number of seconds under which the output becomes `"just now"`. Default: `45`.

- `locale`  
  Reserved for future localization support.

#### Returns

A string such as:

- `"just now"`
- `"1 minute ago"`
- `"in 3 hours"`

## Examples

```js
formatRelative(Date.now() - 1000);
// "just now"

formatRelative(Date.now() - 60 * 1000);
// "1 minute ago"

formatRelative(Date.now() + 60 * 60 * 1000);
// "in 1 hour"
```

## Browser Support

Works in all modern browsers.

## Node.js Support

Supports Node.js 14 and newer.

## Why tiny-date?

Sometimes you don’t need a big date library just to say how long ago something happened.  
**tiny-date** keeps it simple.

## License

MIT

## Contributing

Contributions are welcome! Feel free to open issues and pull requests.

## Roadmap

- More locale support
- Custom wording templates
- Calendar-style relative formatting

## Example Implementation

```js
export function formatRelative(input, options = {}) {
  const now = options.now ?? Date.now();
  const date = input instanceof Date ? input.getTime() : new Date(input).getTime();
  const diffMs = date - now;
  const diffSec = Math.round(Math.abs(diffMs) / 1000);

  if (diffSec < (options.justNowThreshold ?? 45)) return "just now";

  const units = [
    ["year", 60 * 60 * 24 * 365],
    ["month", 60 * 60 * 24 * 30],
    ["day", 60 * 60 * 24],
    ["hour", 60 * 60],
    ["minute", 60],
    ["second", 1],
  ];

  for (const [name, seconds] of units) {
    if (diffSec >= seconds) {
      const value = Math.floor(diffSec / seconds);
      return diffMs < 0 ? `${value} ${name}${value === 1 ? "" : "s"} ago` : `in ${value} ${name}${value === 1 ? "" : "s"}`;
    }
  }

  return "just now";
}
```

## Features

- Lints one or more YAML files
- Recursively scans directories
- Ignores common generated/vendor paths
- Prints clear, actionable error messages
- Designed to be fast and easy to use in scripts and CI

## Installation

### Using Homebrew

```bash
brew install flak
```

### Using Cargo

```bash
cargo install flak
```

### Using Go

```bash
go install github.com/yourorg/flak@latest
```

### From source

```bash
git clone https://github.com/yourorg/flak.git
cd flak
make install
```

## Usage

Lint a single file:

```bash
flak config.yaml
```

Lint multiple files:

```bash
flak a.yaml b.yaml c.yaml
```

Lint a directory recursively:

```bash
flak ./configs
```

### Exit codes

- `0` — No lint errors found
- `1` — Lint errors were found
- `2` — Invalid usage or internal error

## Command-line options

```bash
flak [options] <path>...
```

Common options:

- `-h, --help` — Show help
- `-v, --version` — Show version
- `-q, --quiet` — Suppress non-error output
- `-r, --recursive` — Recurse into directories
- `-i, --ignore <pattern>` — Ignore files or paths matching a pattern
- `--stdin` — Read YAML from standard input

## Examples

### Check a file in CI

```bash
flak ./config/app.yaml
```

### Lint all YAML files in a repo

```bash
find . -name '*.yml' -o -name '*.yaml' | xargs flak
```

### Read from stdin

```bash
cat config.yaml | flak --stdin
```

## Configuration

`flak` can be configured via a config file, for example `.flak.yml`:

```yaml
ignore:
  - vendor/
  - dist/
  - "*.generated.yaml"

rules:
  indentation: 2
  document-start: true
  trailing-spaces: true
```

> Note: Adjust this section to match the actual configuration format supported by `flak`.

## Rules

Depending on your configuration, `flak` may check for things like:

- Invalid YAML syntax
- Inconsistent indentation
- Trailing whitespace
- Duplicate keys
- Missing document start markers
- Tabs in indentation

## Integrations

`flak` is easy to use in CI pipelines:

### GitHub Actions

```yaml
name: YAML Lint

on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  lint:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Install flak
        run: cargo install flak
      - name: Lint YAML
        run: flak .
```

### pre-commit

```yaml
repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/yourorg/flak
    rev: v1.0.0
    hooks:
      - id: flak
```

4. Run the test suite
5. Open a pull request

A tiny React UI component library with 12 small, composable primitives.

## Why paw?

`paw` is designed for building interfaces with minimal ceremony:

- **Small primitives** — focused components that do one thing well
- **Composable** — build larger UI patterns from simple pieces
- **Accessible by default** — semantics and keyboard support where applicable
- **Lightweight** — no heavy framework opinions
- **React-first** — easy to drop into existing apps

```bash
npm install paw
```

or

```bash
yarn add paw
```

or

```bash
pnpm add paw
```

```tsx
import { Button, Card, Input } from "paw";

export function SignupForm() {
  return (
    <Card>
      <Input label="Email" type="email" placeholder="you@example.com" />
      <Input label="Password" type="password" />
      <Button>Sign up</Button>
    </Card>
  );
}
```

`paw` includes 12 small UI primitives:

1. **Button** — clickable actions
2. **Card** — surface container
3. **Input** — text entry field
4. **Label** — field label
5. **Checkbox** — boolean toggle
6. **Radio** — single-choice input
7. **Select** — dropdown selection
8. **Switch** — on/off toggle
9. **Badge** — small status indicator
10. **Avatar** — user image or fallback
11. **Tooltip** — contextual helper text

import {

  Badge,
  Button,
  Card,
  Checkbox,
  Divider,
  Input,
  Label,
  Radio,
  Select,
  Switch,
  Tooltip,

      <Badge>Pro</Badge>

      <Label htmlFor="name">Name</Label>

      <Tooltip content="This setting is visible to other users.">

      </Tooltip>

      <Divider />
    </Card>
  );
}

- **Clear props**
- **Easy to style**
- **Predictable behavior**
- **Minimal API surface**

- CSS Modules
- Tailwind CSS
- Styled Components
- Emotion
- plain CSS

# paw

A tiny React component library of 12 small UI primitives.

Built for fast product work, paw gives you a minimal set of accessible, composable components that are easy to style and easy to ship.

## Features

- 12 focused UI primitives
- React-first API
- Small, composable, and opinionated where it helps
- Accessible by default
- Lightweight and easy to theme
- Designed to work well in design systems and internal apps

## Installation

```bash
npm install paw
```

or

```bash
yarn add paw
```

or

```bash
pnpm add paw
```

## Usage

```tsx
import {
  Button,
  Badge,
  Card,
  Checkbox,
  Dialog,
  Input,
  Label,
  Menu,
  Modal,
  Progress,
  Switch,
  Tooltip,
} from "paw";

export function Example() {
  return (
    <Card>
      <Label htmlFor="email">Email</Label>
      <Input id="email" placeholder="you@example.com" />

      <Checkbox>Subscribe to updates</Checkbox>
      <Switch>Enable notifications</Switch>

      <Button>Save</Button>
    </Card>
  );
}
```

## Components

paw includes 12 small primitives:

1. **Button** — primary action control
2. **Badge** — compact status label
3. **Card** — framed content container
4. **Checkbox** — boolean input
5. **Dialog** — modal dialog
6. **Input** — text input
7. **Label** — form label
8. **Menu** — simple action menu
9. **Modal** — overlay container
10. **Progress** — progress indicator
11. **Switch** — toggle control
12. **Tooltip** — contextual hint

## Philosophy

paw is intentionally small.

Instead of trying to replace a full design system, paw focuses on the building blocks that most apps need every day. The goal is to keep the API predictable and the implementation easy to understand.

## Styling

All components are designed to be styled with your preferred approach:

- CSS Modules
- Tailwind CSS
- vanilla CSS
- CSS-in-JS

You can theme paw by overriding class names, tokens, or component styles depending on your setup.

## Accessibility

Accessibility is a core goal of paw.

We aim to provide sensible defaults for:

- keyboard navigation
- focus handling
- semantic markup
- screen reader compatibility

Always test the components in your application context to make sure they meet your specific accessibility needs.

```tsx
<Button onClick={() => alert("Saved!")}>Save</Button>

```tsx
<Dialog open={open} onOpenChange={setOpen}>

    This action cannot be undone.

  <Dialog.Footer>
    <Button variant="secondary" onClick={() => setOpen(false)}>
      Cancel
    </Button>
    <Button variant="danger" onClick={handleDelete}>
      Delete
    </Button>
  </Dialog.Footer>
</Dialog>
```

### Tooltip

```tsx
<Tooltip content="Copy to clipboard">
  <Button>Copy</Button>
</Tooltip>
```

## Roadmap

Possible future additions:

- more form primitives
- improved theming support
- motion utilities
- documentation site
- example app

## Contributing

Contributions are welcome.

1. Fork the repository
2. Create a feature branch
3. Make your changes
4. Open a pull request

## License

MIT

Of course! Here is a complete `README.md` for a small open-source library called `tiny-date`.

This README is designed to be clear, concise, and welcoming to potential users and contributors. It highlights the library's key selling points (small size, no dependencies) and provides easy-to-follow examples.

---

# tiny-date

[![npm version](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/tiny-date.svg)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/tiny-date)
[![bundle size](https://img.shields.io/bundlephobia/minzip/tiny-date.svg)](https://bundlephobia.com/result?p=tiny-date)
[![license](https://img.shields.io/npm/l/tiny-date.svg)](https://opensource.org/licenses/MIT)

A tiny (**<1KB**), zero-dependency, human-readable date formatter.

Tired of heavy date libraries like Moment.js or date-fns for simple "time ago" formatting? `tiny-date` is the answer. It does one thing and does it well: it gives you a human-friendly, relative time string.

- "just now"
- "5 minutes ago"
- "yesterday"
- "in 2 weeks"
- "3 months ago"

## ✨ Features

- **Super Lightweight**: Less than 1KB gzipped.
- **Zero Dependencies**: Drop it in any project without extra baggage.
- **Simple API**: A single function to learn.
- **Handles Past & Future**: Formats dates both in the past ("ago") and in the future ("in").
- **Flexible Input**: Accepts Date objects, timestamps, or ISO strings.
- **Customizable & i18n**: Easily override the default English strings for internationalization.

## 📦 Installation

```bash
# Using npm
npm install tiny-date

# Using yarn
yarn add tiny-date
```

## 🚀 Usage

Import the function and pass it a date. It will automatically compare it to `now`.

```javascript
import tinyDate from 'tiny-date';

// Works with Date objects
const fiveMinutesAgo = new Date(Date.now() - 5 * 60 * 1000);
console.log(tinyDate(fiveMinutesAgo));
// => "5 minutes ago"

const inTwoWeeks = new Date(Date.now() + 14 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000);
console.log(tinyDate(inTwoWeeks));
// => "in 2 weeks"

// Works with timestamps (milliseconds)
const oneHourAgo = Date.now() - 60 * 60 * 1000;
console.log(tinyDate(oneHourAgo));
// => "an hour ago"

// Works with ISO strings
const yesterday = '2023-10-26T12:00:00.000Z'; // Assuming today is 2023-10-27
console.log(tinyDate(yesterday));
// => "yesterday"
```

### Example Outputs

| Time Difference        | Output             |
| ---------------------- | ------------------ |
| 0-45 seconds           | "just now"         |
| 45-90 seconds          | "a minute ago"     |
| 2-45 minutes           | "X minutes ago"    |
| 45-90 minutes          | "an hour ago"      |
| 2-22 hours             | "X hours ago"      |
| 22-36 hours            | "yesterday"        |
| 2-7 days               | "X days ago"       |
| 8-14 days              | "last week"        |
| 15-25 days             | "X weeks ago"      |
| 26-45 days             | "last month"       |
| 45 days - 10 months    | "X months ago"     |
| 10-18 months           | "last year"        |
| 1.5+ years             | "X years ago"      |

*(Future dates follow a similar pattern, e.g., "in 5 minutes", "tomorrow", "in 2 weeks").*

## ⚙️ API

### `tinyDate(date, [now])`

-   **`date`**: `Date | number | string` (Required)
    The date to format. Can be a `Date` object, a millisecond timestamp, or a string parsable by `new Date()`.

-   **`now`**: `Date | number` (Optional)
    A reference date to compare against. Defaults to `Date.now()`. Useful for testing or specific use cases.

    ```javascript
    const customNow = new Date('2023-01-15');
    const targetDate = new Date('2023-01-01');

    console.log(tinyDate(targetDate, customNow));
    // => "2 weeks ago"
    ```

## 🌍 Customization & Internationalization (i18n)

You can easily customize the output for different languages or wording preferences by using the `setOptions` method.

```javascript
import tinyDate from 'tiny-date';

// Example for Spanish localization
tinyDate.setOptions({
  now: 'ahora mismo',
  past: 'hace %s',
  future: 'en %s',
  singular: {
    s: 'un segundo',
    m: 'un minuto',
    h: 'una hora',
    d: 'un día',
    w: 'una semana',
    mo: 'un mes',
    y: 'un año',
  },

Displaying human-readable, relative timestamps is a common UI requirement. `tiny-date` provides a simple and lightweight solution without pulling in a large date-manipulation library. It's incredibly small (~1KB gzipped), making it perfect for projects where bundle size is a concern.

-   **Tiny Footprint**: Less than 1KB gzipped.
-   **Zero Dependencies**: Plain JavaScript, no external libraries needed.
-   **Simple API**: A single function to learn.
-   **Future & Past**: Handles both past ("3 hours ago") and future ("in 3 hours") dates.
-   **Customizable**: Easily override the default output strings.
-   **Internationalization (i18n)**: Full support for any language via customization.
-   **Universal**: Works in Node.js and all modern browsers.

## Installation

Install via your favorite package manager:

```bash
npm install tiny-date
```

or

```bash
yarn add tiny-date
```

### Browser / CDN

You can also use it directly in the browser via a CDN:

```html
<script src="https://unpkg.com/tiny-date/dist/tiny-date.min.js"></script>
<script>
  // The function is available on the window object
  const timeAgo = tinydate(new Date(Date.now() - 5000));
  console.log(timeAgo); // => 'just now'
</script>
```

## Usage

Import the function and pass it a `Date` object, a timestamp, or a date string.

```javascript
import tinydate from 'tiny-date';

// A few seconds ago
tinydate(new Date(Date.now() - 5000));
// => 'just now'

// 10 minutes ago
tinydate(new Date(Date.now() - 1000 * 60 * 10));
// => '10 minutes ago'

// 1 hour ago
tinydate(new Date(Date.now() - 1000 * 60 * 60));
// => '1 hour ago'

// Yesterday
tinydate(new Date(Date.now() - 1000 * 60 * 60 * 24));
// => 'yesterday'

// In the future
tinydate(new Date(Date.now() + 1000 * 60 * 60 * 24 * 3));
// => 'in 3 days'

// From a timestamp (number)
tinydate(Date.now() - 1000 * 60 * 60 * 24 * 7);
// => '1 week ago'

// From a date string
tinydate('2023-01-01T12:00:00Z');
// (assuming 'now' is much later) => 'on Jan 1, 2023'
```

## API

### `tinydate(date, [options])`

#### `date`

Type: `Date | number | string`
**Required**

The date to format. Can be a `Date` object, a Unix timestamp (milliseconds), or a string parsable by `new Date()`.

#### `options`

Type: `object`
*Optional*

An object to customize the output.

| Option  | Type     | Default                               | Description                                                                                             |
| :------ | :------- | :------------------------------------ | :------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `now`   | `number` | `Date.now()`                          | A custom "now" timestamp in milliseconds. Useful for testing or server-side rendering.                  |
| `strings` | `object` | [See default strings](#customization) | An object containing custom strings to override the defaults, enabling translation and customization. |

## Customization & Internationalization (i18n)

You can easily customize the output or translate it into another language by passing a `strings` object in the options. You only need to provide the keys you want to override.

Here is the default `strings` object:

```javascript
const defaultStrings = {
  prefixAgo: null,
  prefixFromNow: 'in',
  suffixAgo: 'ago',
  suffixFromNow: null,
  seconds: 'less than a minute',
  minute: '1 minute',
  minutes: '%d minutes',
  hour: '1 hour',
  hours: '%d hours',
  day: '1 day',
  days: '%d days',
  week: '1 week',
  weeks: '%d weeks',
  month: '1 month',
  months: '%d months',
  year: '1 year',
  years: '%d years',
  wordSeparator: ' ',
  justNow: 'just now',
  yesterday: 'yesterday',
  tomorrow: 'tomorrow',
  // Function to format dates that are too far in the past or future
  // Receives a Date object.
  onDate: (date) => {
    const month = date.toLocaleString('default', { month: 'short' });
    return `on ${month} ${date.getDate()}, ${date.getFullYear()}`;
  },
};
```

  prefixAgo: 'hace',
  prefixFromNow: 'en',
  suffixAgo: null,
  suffixFromNow: null,
  seconds: 'menos de un minuto',
  minute: '1 minuto',
  minutes: '%d minutos',
  hour: '1 hora',
  hours: '%d horas',
  day: '1 día',
  days: '%d días',
  week: '1 semana',
  weeks: '%d semanas',
  month: '1 mes',
  months: '%d meses',
  year: '1 año',
  years: '%d años',
  justNow: 'ahora mismo',
  yesterday: 'ayer',
  tomorrow: 'mañana',
  onDate: (date) => {
    return `el ${date.getDate()} de ${date.toLocaleString('es', { month: 'long' })} de ${date.getFullYear()}`;
  }
};

const fiveMinutesAgo = new Date(Date.now() - 1000 * 60 * 5);
const twoWeeksFromNow = new Date(Date.now() + 1000 * 60 * 60 * 24 * 14);

tinydate(fiveMinutesAgo, { strings: spanishStrings });
// => 'hace 5 minutos'

tinydate(twoWeeksFromNow, { strings: spanishStrings });
// => 'en 2 semanas'
```

# tiny-date

[![NPM Version](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/tiny-date.svg)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/tiny-date)
[![Build Status](https://img.shields.io/github/actions/workflow/status/your-username/tiny-date/ci.yml?branch=main)](https://github.com/your-username/tiny-date/actions)
[![Bundle Size](https://img.shields.io/bundlephobia/minzip/tiny-date.svg)](https://bundlephobia.com/result?p=tiny-date)
[![License](https://img.shields.io/npm/l/tiny-date.svg)](https://github.com/your-username/tiny-date/blob/main/LICENSE)

A tiny, zero-dependency library for elegantly formatting dates relative to now.

Ever needed to display "posted 5 minutes ago" or "event starts in 2 weeks" without pulling in a heavy date library? `tiny-date` is your solution. It's fast, lightweight, and does one thing well.

```js
import tinydate from 'tiny-date';

const fiveMinutesAgo = new Date(Date.now() - 1000 * 60 * 5);
tinydate(fiveMinutesAgo);
// => '5 minutes ago'

const inTwoWeeks = new Date(Date.now() + 1000 * 60 * 60 * 24 * 14);
tinydate(inTwoWeeks);
// => 'in 2 weeks'
```

## ✨ Features

- **Extremely Lightweight:** Less than 1KB minified and gzipped.
- **Zero Dependencies:** No other packages needed. Drop it in and go.
- **Simple, Intuitive API:** One main function handles everything.
- **Supports Past & Future:** Formats dates both in the past ("ago") and in the future ("in").
- **Smart Formatting:** Automatically uses the most appropriate unit (e.g., seconds, minutes, hours, yesterday, weeks, months, years).
- **Customizable & i18n:** Easily override the default English strings for internationalization.

## 🚀 Installation

Install using your favorite package manager:

```bash
# npm
npm install tiny-date

# yarn
yarn add tiny-date

# pnpm
pnpm add tiny-date
```

You can also use it directly in the browser via a CDN:

```html
<script src="https://unpkg.com/tiny-date/dist/tiny-date.min.js"></script>
<script>
  const formattedDate = tinydate(new Date());
  console.log(formattedDate);
</script>
```

## Usage

The library exports a single default function. Import it, pass in a date, and get a human-readable string back.

```js
import tinydate from 'tiny-date';

// Past dates
tinydate(Date.now() - 3000);              // 'just now'
tinydate(Date.now() - 1000 * 45);         // '45 seconds ago'
tinydate(Date.now() - 1000 * 60 * 30);    // '30 minutes ago'
tinydate(Date.now() - 1000 * 60 * 60 * 8); // '8 hours ago'
tinydate(Date.now() - 1000 * 60 * 60 * 25); // 'yesterday'
tinydate(Date.now() - 1000 * 60 * 60 * 24 * 5); // '5 days ago'
tinydate(Date.now() - 1000 * 60 * 60 * 24 * 35); // '1 month ago'
tinydate(Date.now() - 1000 * 60 * 60 * 24 * 400); // '1 year ago'

// Future dates
tinydate(Date.now() + 1000 * 60);         // 'in 1 minute'
tinydate(Date.now() + 1000 * 60 * 60);    // 'in 1 hour'
tinydate(Date.now() + 1000 * 60 * 60 * 24); // 'tomorrow'
tinydate(Date.now() + 1000 * 60 * 60 * 24 * 14); // 'in 2 weeks'
tinydate(Date.now() + 1000 * 60 * 60 * 24 * 365 * 2); // 'in 2 years'
```

### Using a custom "now"

For testing or specific use cases, you can provide a custom reference date instead of `Date.now()`.

```js
const myDate = new Date('2023-10-26T10:00:00Z');
const customNow = new Date('2023-10-26T10:05:00Z');

tinydate(myDate, { now: customNow });
// => '5 minutes ago'
```

## 📖 API Reference

### `tinydate(date, [options])`

#### `date`

Type: `Date | number | string`

The date to format. Can be a `Date` object, a Unix timestamp (milliseconds), or a string parsable by `new Date()`.

#### `options` (optional)

Type: `object`

An object for configuring the output.

##### `options.now`

Type: `Date | number`
Default: `Date.now()`

A reference date to calculate the difference from.

##### `options.locales`

Type: `object`
Default: English locales

An object to override the default strings for internationalization (i18n). See the [Internationalization](#-internationalization-i18n) section for a full example.

The structure is as follows:

```js
{
  now: 'just now',
  past: '{n} {unit} ago', // or a function: (n, unit) => `${n} ${unit} ago`
  future: 'in {n} {unit}', // or a function: (n, unit) => `in ${n} ${unit}`
  units: {
    second: { single: 'second', plural: 'seconds' },
    minute: { single: 'minute', plural: 'minutes' },
    hour: { single: 'hour', plural: 'hours' },
    day: { single: 'day', plural: 'days', special: { '-1': 'yesterday', '1': 'tomorrow' } },
    week: { single: 'week', plural: 'weeks' },
    month: { single: 'month', plural: 'months' },
    year: { single: 'year', plural: 'years' },
  }
}
```

## 🌍 Internationalization (i18n)

You can easily format dates for different languages by passing a `locales` object in the options.

Here is an example for Spanish:

```js
import tinydate from 'tiny-date';

const esLocale = {
  now: 'ahora mismo',
  past: 'hace {n} {unit}',
  future: 'en {n} {unit}',
  units: {
    second: { single: 'segundo', plural: 'segundos' },
    minute: { single: 'minuto', plural: 'minutos' },
    hour: { single: 'hora', plural: 'horas' },
    day: { single: 'día', plural: 'días', special: { '-1': 'ayer', '1': 'mañana' } },
    week: { single: 'semana', plural: 'semanas' },
    month: { single: 'mes', plural: 'meses' },
    year: { single: 'año', plural: 'años' },
  }
};

const date = new Date(Date.now() - 1000 * 60 * 30);

tinydate(date, { locales: esLocale });
// => 'hace 30 minutos'
```

## 🤔 Why another date library?

Libraries like `moment.js`, `date-fns`, and `day.js` are fantastic, feature-rich tools. However, they can be overkill if you *only* need relative time formatting. `tiny-date` is for those moments when bundle size is critical and you need a focused, performant solution without any extra weight.

It's the difference between a full-featured kitchen appliance and a sharp, reliable paring knife. Both are useful, but you don't always need the big one.

# tiny-date

[![NPM Version](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/tiny-date.svg)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/tiny-date)
[![Bundle Size](https://img.shields.io/bundlephobia/minzip/tiny-date.svg)](https://bundlephobia.com/result?p=tiny-date)

[![License](https://img.shields.io/npm/l/tiny-date.svg)](https://github.com/your-username/tiny-date/blob/main/LICENSE)

A tiny, zero-dependency JavaScript library for creating human-readable, relative time strings.

Instead of showing a full timestamp like `2023-10-27T10:00:00Z`, you can display friendly formats like `5 minutes ago`, `yesterday`, or `in 2 weeks`. It's perfect for projects where bundle size is a critical concern.

## Features

-   **📦 Tiny:** Less than 1KB gzipped.
-   **🚀 Zero Dependencies:** No other packages needed to run.
-   **✨ Simple API:** A single, easy-to-use function.
-   **↔️ Past & Future:** Handles both past and future dates seamlessly.
-   **🌍 i18n Ready:** Easily customize the output for different languages.
-   **✅ Well-Tested:** Robust and reliable.

## Installation

Install using your favorite package manager:

```bash
# Using npm
npm install tiny-date

# Using yarn
yarn add tiny-date

# Using pnpm
pnpm add tiny-date
```

You can also use it directly in the browser via a CDN:

```html
<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/tiny-date/dist/tiny-date.min.js"></script>
```

## Usage

Import the function and pass it a `Date` object, a timestamp, or a valid date string.

```javascript
import tinydate from 'tiny-date';

// Pass a Date object
const fiveMinutesAgo = new Date(Date.now() - 5 * 60 * 1000);
console.log(tinydate(fiveMinutesAgo));
//=> "5 minutes ago"

// Pass a timestamp (milliseconds)
const twoHoursFromNow = Date.now() + 2 * 60 * 60 * 1000;
console.log(tinydate(twoHoursFromNow));
//=> "in 2 hours"

// Pass a date string
console.log(tinydate('2022-01-01'));
//=> "2 years ago" (assuming today is in 2024)
```

### Examples

```javascript
import tinydate from 'tiny-date';

// Past
tinydate(new Date(Date.now() - 10 * 1000));      // "just now"
tinydate(new Date(Date.now() - 45 * 1000));      // "45 seconds ago"
tinydate(new Date(Date.now() - 5 * 60 * 1000));   // "5 minutes ago"
tinydate(new Date(Date.now() - 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000)); // "yesterday"
tinydate(new Date(Date.now() - 6 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000)); // "6 days ago"
tinydate(new Date(Date.now() - 3 * 30 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000)); // "3 months ago"

// Future
tinydate(new Date(Date.now() + 60 * 1000));      // "in 1 minute"
tinydate(new Date(Date.now() + 2 * 60 * 60 * 1000)); // "in 2 hours"
tinydate(new Date(Date.now() + 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000)); // "tomorrow"
tinydate(new Date(Date.now() + 15 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000)); // "in 2 weeks"
tinydate(new Date(Date.now() + 365 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000)); // "in 1 year"
```

## API

### `tinydate(date, [options])`

Returns a `string` representing the relative time.

#### `date`

Type: `Date | number | string`
**Required**

The date to format. Can be a `Date` object, a Unix timestamp in milliseconds, or a string parseable by `new Date()`.

#### `options`

Type: `object`
**Optional**

An object to customize the output.

##### `options.now`

Type: `Date | number`
Default: `new Date()`

A custom "now" reference date. This is useful for testing or for situations where you need to calculate relative time against a fixed point.

```javascript
const customNow = new Date('2023-01-15');
const date = new Date('2023-01-10');

tinydate(date, { now: customNow });
//=> "5 days ago"
```

##### `options.locales`

Type: `object`
Default: English locales

An object to override the default strings for internationalization (i18n). See the [Internationalization](#internationalization) section for details.

## Internationalization (i18n)

You can easily format dates for different languages by providing a `locales` object in the options.

Here is an example for Spanish:

```javascript

const spanishLocales = {
  now: 'ahora mismo',
  second: 'segundo',
  minute: 'minuto',
  hour: 'hora',
  day: 'día',
  week: 'semana',
  month: 'mes',
  year: 'año',
  ago: 'hace %s',
  in: 'en %s',
  yesterday: 'ayer',
  tomorrow: 'mañana',
  plural: 's'
};

const date = new Date(Date.now() - 5 * 60 * 1000);

console.log(tinydate(date, { locales: spanishLocales }));
//=> "hace 5 minutos"
```

The `%s` in `ago` and `in` is a placeholder that will be replaced by the time string (e.g., "5 minutos"). The `plural` key is a string that will be appended to the unit when the value is not `1`.

## ✨ Features

-   **Ultra-lightweight:** Around 300 bytes gzipped, perfect for performance-critical applications.
-   **Zero Dependencies:** No other packages to worry about.
-   **Simple API:** A single function is all you need.
-   **Supports Past and Future:** Formats dates both in the past ("3 hours ago") and in the future ("in 5 minutes").
-   **Customizable:** Easily extend with your own language translations (i18n).

## 🚀 Installation

## Usage

The most common use case is to import the `format` function and pass it a `Date` object, a timestamp, or a date string.

```javascript
import { format } from 'tiny-date';

// Using a Date object
const oneHourAgo = new Date(Date.now() - 60 * 60 * 1000);
console.log(format(oneHourAgo));
//=> "an hour ago"

// Using a timestamp (milliseconds)

console.log(format(yesterday));
//=> "yesterday"

// Using an ISO string

console.log(format(twoWeeksAgo));
//=> "2 weeks ago"

// Future dates work too!

console.log(format(inFiveMinutes));
//=> "in 5 minutes"
```

### More Examples

# ❄️ flak

**A blazingly fast, configurable linter for your YAML files.**

[![Build Status](https://img.shields.io/travis/com/your-username/flak.svg?style=flat-square)](https://travis-ci.com/your-username/flak)
[![PyPI Version](https://img.shields.io/pypi/v/flak-linter.svg?style=flat-square)](https://pypi.org/project/flak-linter/)
[![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-yellow.svg?style=flat-square)](https://opensource.org/licenses/MIT)
[![Downloads](https://img.shields.io/pypi/dm/flak-linter.svg?style=flat-square)](https://pypi.org/project/flak-linter/)

`flak` helps you enforce consistent styles and catch common errors in your YAML files. Whether you're managing Kubernetes configs, GitHub Actions workflows, or application settings, `flak` ensures your YAML is clean, correct, and maintainable.

## Why `flak`?

YAML is designed to be human-readable, but it's notoriously prone to subtle syntax errors like indentation issues, duplicate keys, or incorrect boolean values. `flak` automates the process of finding these problems so you can focus on what matters.

-   **Fast:** Built with performance in mind to run quickly in your CI/CD pipelines.
-   **Configurable:** Don't like a rule? Turn it off. Need a different indent style? Change it.
-   **Auto-fixable:** `flak` can automatically fix many common issues, saving you time.
-   **CI/CD Friendly:** Use it in pre-commit hooks or your CI pipeline to maintain code quality.

## Features

-   ✅ **Comprehensive Rules:** Checks for correctness, style, and best practices.
-   🔧 **Smart Auto-fix:** Run `flak --fix` to automatically correct errors like indentation, quotes, and more.
-   ⚙️ **Zero-Config Ready:** Works out of the box with sensible defaults.
-   📄 **Flexible Configuration:** Customize rules, severity, and ignored files via a `.flak.yml` file.
-   🎨 **Multiple Output Formats:** Supports human-readable text, JSON, and Checkstyle for easy integration.

## Installation

You can install `flak` using pip:

```bash
pip install flak-linter
```

Alternatively, you can use Homebrew on macOS:

```bash
brew install your-username/tap/flak
```

## Usage

Lint a single file, multiple files, or an entire directory.

```bash
# Lint a single file
flak config.yml

# Lint multiple files
flak service-a.yml service-b.yml

# Lint all YAML files in a directory (recursively)
flak .

# Automatically fix problems
flak --fix path/to/your/yaml/
```

### Command-line Options

```
$ flak --help
Usage: flak [OPTIONS] [PATHS]...

  A blazingly fast, configurable linter for your YAML files.

Options:
  --fix                 Automatically fix fixable errors.
  --config FILE         Path to a custom configuration file.
  --format [text|json|checkstyle]
                        The output format for the results.
  --version             Show the version and exit.
  --help                Show this message and exit.
```

## Configuration

For project-specific settings, create a `.flak.yml` file in your project's root directory.

Here is an example configuration:

```yaml
# .flak.yml

# Inherit from a recommended ruleset
extends: recommended

# Define files/directories to ignore
ignore:
  - 'node_modules/'
  - 'vendor/'

# Customize specific rules
rules:
  # Enforce 2-space indentation (error level)
  indentation: [error, {width: 2}]

  # Warn about lines longer than 80 characters
  line-length: [warn, {max: 80}]

  # Require single quotes for strings
  quotes: [error, {style: single}]

  # Disable the check for trailing spaces
  trailing-spaces: off
```

`flak` will automatically find and use `.flak.yml` if it exists in the current directory or any parent directory.

## Example

Given a problematic YAML file `deployment.yml`:

```yaml
# deployment.yml
apiVersion: "apps/v1"
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: my-app
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: my-app
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: "my-app"
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: server
        image: my-image:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
# Duplicate key!
metadata:
  name: my-app-duplicate
```

Running `flak` would produce the following output:

```
$ flak deployment.yml

deployment.yml
  1:1   error    Expected 2-space indentation, but found 0.  (indentation)
  2:12  warning  String "apps/v1" should be in single quotes. (quotes)
  17:1  error    Duplicate key "metadata" found.             (key-duplicates)

✖ 3 problems (2 errors, 1 warning)
```

Running with `--fix` would correct the fixable issues:

```bash
flak --fix deployment.yml
```

The file would be changed to:

```yaml
# deployment.yml
apiVersion: 'apps/v1'
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: my-app
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: my-app
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: 'my-app'
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: server
          image: my-image:latest
          ports:
            - containerPort: 80
# Duplicate key!
metadata:
  name: my-app-duplicate
```
*(Note: The duplicate key error cannot be fixed automatically and would still be reported.)*

# ❄️ flak

**A simple, fast, and opinionated linter for your YAML files.**

`flak` helps you write clean, consistent, and error-free YAML. Whether you're managing Kubernetes configs, GitHub Actions workflows, or Ansible playbooks, `flak` catches common mistakes and enforces best practices, so you can avoid frustrating deployment and parsing errors.

## Why `flak`?

-   **Fast:** Built with performance in mind to lint large codebases in seconds.
-   **Simple:** Zero-config by default. Just run `flak .` and you're good to go.
-   **Auto-fixable:** Supports a `--fix` flag to automatically correct many common issues.
-   **Configurable:** Easily extend or override rules via a simple `.flak.yaml` file.
-   **CI/CD Friendly:** Designed to be a seamless addition to your continuous integration pipelines.

## Features

-   ✅ **Syntax Validation:** Catches fundamental YAML syntax errors.
-   🔑 **Duplicate Key Detection:** Finds duplicate keys within the same mapping.
-   💅 **Style Enforcement:** Checks for consistent indentation, quoting, and spacing.
-   🧐 **Best Practices:** Warns about "truthy" values (like `on`, `no`) that can be misinterpreted as booleans.
-   -o- **Auto-fixing:** Automatically corrects issues like trailing whitespace, indentation, and more.
-   📂 **Recursive Discovery:** Scans directories for `.yml` and `.yaml` files automatically.

## Installation

You can install `flak` using pip:

```bash
pip install flak-linter
```

Alternatively, you can use `pipx` to install it in an isolated environment:

```bash
pipx install flak-linter
```

## Usage

Lint a single file:

```bash
flak config.yaml
```

Lint all YAML files in a directory recursively:

```bash
flak my-project/
```

Lint the current directory:

```bash
flak .
```

### Auto-fixing Problems

To automatically fix issues that are correctable, use the `--fix` flag:

```bash
flak --fix my-project/
```

### Command-Line Options

```
Usage: flak [OPTIONS] [PATHS]...

  A simple, fast, and opinionated linter for your YAML files.

Options:
  --fix              Automatically fix linting errors.
  --config FILE      Path to a custom configuration file.
  --format [text|json|github]
                     Output format for linting results.
  --version          Show the version and exit.
  --help             Show this message and exit.
```

## Configuration

For most projects, `flak` works out of the box. To customize its behavior, create a `.flak.yaml` file in your project's root directory.

`flak` will automatically discover configuration files in this order:
1.  `.flak.yaml`
2.  `.flak.yml`
3.  `pyproject.toml` (in the `[tool.flak]` section)

#### Example `.flak.yaml`

```yaml
# .flak.yaml

# You can extend a shared configuration (future feature)
# extends: recommended

# Specify files/directories to ignore
exclude:
  - "node_modules/"
  - "vendor/"
  - "**/__snapshots__/"

# Configure specific rules
rules:
  # Set indentation to 4 spaces instead of the default 2
  indentation:
    level: 4
    
  # Disable a rule entirely
  trailing-whitespace: off
  
  # Change a rule's severity to a warning
  key-quotes:
    level: warn
    style: "consistent" # 'consistent' or 'unquoted'
```

## Example

Given a problematic YAML file `ci.yaml`:

```yaml
# ci.yaml
jobs:
  build:
    image: 'ubuntu-latest'
    steps:
    - name: Checkout
      uses: actions/checkout@v2
    - name: Run tests
      run: |
        npm install
        npm test
  deploy:
    image: 'ubuntu-latest'
    needs: build
    # This key is duplicated!
    needs: lint 
```

Running `flak ci.yaml` would produce the following output:

```
ci.yaml
  13:5  error  Duplicate key "needs" found in mapping  (duplicate-keys)

✖ 1 problem (1 error, 0 warnings)
```

| `duplicate-keys`      | Prevents duplicate keys from being used in the same mapping. |      -       |
| `indentation`         | Enforces a consistent indentation width (default: 2 spaces). |      ✅      |
| `trailing-whitespace` | Disallows trailing whitespace on lines.                      |      ✅      |
| `truthy-values`       | Warns about unquoted strings like `on`, `off`, `yes`, `no`.  |      -       |
| `key-quotes`          | Enforces a consistent style for quoting keys.                |      ✅      |
| `max-line-length`     | Enforces a maximum line length (default: 120).               |      -       |
| `empty-lines`         | Limits the number of consecutive empty lines.                |      ✅      |

## Features

-   **Comprehensive Rule Set:** Checks for everything from syntax errors and duplicate keys to stylistic issues like indentation and line length.
-   **Highly Configurable:** Use a simple `.flak.yaml` file to enable/disable rules, set severity levels, and ignore specific files.
-   **CI/CD Friendly:** Exits with a non-zero status code when issues are found, making it perfect for integrating into your pipelines.
-   **Fast:** Built with performance in mind to lint large codebases in seconds.
-   **Multiple Output Formats:** Supports human-readable text, JSON, and checkstyle formats for easy integration with other tools.
-   **Stdin Support:** Lint YAML from pipes and other command-line utilities.

## Installation

The recommended way to install `flak` is using `pipx` to ensure it's installed in an isolated environment.

```bash
pipx install flak
```

Alternatively, you can install it with `pip`:

```bash
pip install flak
```

### Other Methods

-   **Homebrew (macOS):**
    ```bash
    brew install your-username/tap/flak
    ```
-   **Binaries:**
    Pre-compiled binaries for Linux, macOS, and Windows are available on the [Releases page](https://github.com/your-username/flak/releases).

### Basic Linting

To lint a single file or multiple files:

```bash
flak my-file.yaml
flak service.yaml config/dev.yaml
```

To lint an entire directory recursively:

```bash
flak ./kubernetes/
```

### Example Output

```
./config/service.yaml:12:5: error: Duplicate key "replicas" found. (duplicate-keys)
./config/service.yaml:25:1: warning: Line length should not exceed 88 characters. (line-length)
```

### Linting from stdin

You can pipe content directly to `flak` using `-` as the filename.

```bash
cat my-file.yaml | flak -
kubectl get pod my-pod -o yaml | flak -
```

### Command-Line Options

```bash
flak --help

Usage: flak [OPTIONS] [PATHS]...

  A blazingly fast, configurable, and opinionated linter for your YAML files.

Options:
  -c, --config FILE  Specify a custom configuration file.
  -f, --format TEXT  Output format (text, json, checkstyle). [default: text]
  --version          Show the version and exit.
  --help             Show this message and exit.
```

## Configuration

`flak` is configured using a `.flak.yaml` file in your project's root directory. If no configuration is found, it uses a sensible set of default rules.

To get started, you can create a basic `.flak.yaml` file:

```bash
flak --generate-config > .flak.yaml
```

### `.flak.yaml` Example

Here is an example configuration file that extends the default ruleset, customizes a few rules, and ignores a directory.

```yaml
# .flak.yaml

# Extend the recommended default configuration.
extends: default

# Define custom rule settings.
# You can change the severity level (error, warning) or disable a rule (off).
rules:
  line-length:
    max: 120
    level: warning

  key-case:
    rule: snake_case
    level: error

  indentation: off # Disable the indentation rule entirely

# List of file paths or glob patterns to ignore.
exclude:
  - 'vendor/'
  - '**/tests/fixtures/*.yaml'
```

`flak` comes with a variety of built-in rules. Here are some of the most common ones:

| Rule ID             | Description                                               | Default |

| `indentation`       | Enforces a consistent indentation width (e.g., 2 spaces). | `error` |
| `line-length`       | Enforces a maximum line length.                           | `warning` |
| `trailing-spaces`   | Disallows trailing whitespace on lines.                   | `warning` |
| `key-case`          | Enforces a specific case for keys (e.g., `camelCase`).    | `off`   |
| `truthy-values`     | Warns against using non-boolean strings like "true", "off". | `warning` |
| `empty-lines`       | Checks for an excessive number of consecutive empty lines.  | `warning` |
| `document-start`    | Requires the `---` document start marker.                 | `off`   |

For a full list of rules and their options, please see the [official documentation](https://your-username.github.io/flak/rules/).

YAML is designed to be human-readable, but it's notoriously strict and prone to subtle errors that can be hard to spot. A misplaced indent, a trailing space, or an unquoted boolean can break your application or deployment.

`flak` is designed to be:
- **Fast:** Get feedback in milliseconds, perfect for pre-commit hooks and CI pipelines.
- **Simple:** Zero-config by default. Just run it on your files.
- **Helpful:** Error messages are clear, pointing directly to the line and column with a suggestion for a fix.

- ✅ **Syntax and Style Checking:** Catches everything from duplicate keys to inconsistent indentation.
- ⚙️ **Customizable:** Configure rules, exclude files, and set standards in a `.flak.yml` file.

## Installation

The recommended way to install `flak` is with `pipx` to ensure it's in an isolated environment.

pipx install flak-linter

Alternatively, you can use `pip`:

pip install flak-linter

Lint a single file:

flak config/production.yml

Lint multiple files or use a glob pattern:

flak k8s/*.yaml services/**/*.yml
```

Lint an entire directory recursively:
```bash
flak .
```

Automatically fix correctable errors:
```bash
flak --fix .
```

View all available options:

flak --help

# .flak.yml

# Files and directories to ignore. Supports glob patterns.
exclude:

rules:

## Example Workflow

# deployment.yml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment

spec:

    # ...

Running `flak` on it will produce clear, actionable output:

```bash

```

kind: Deployment
metadata:

    # ...

| `key-duplicates`      | Disallows duplicate keys within the same mapping.  |      ❌      |
| `quoted-booleans`     | Enforces booleans (`true`/`false`) are not quoted. |      ✅      |
| `quoted-numerics`     | Enforces numeric values are not quoted.            |      ✅      |
| `hyphen-spacing`      | Enforces a single space after a list item hyphen.  |      ✅      |
| `line-length`         | Checks for lines exceeding a maximum length.       |      ❌      |

### In Configuration File

To disable a rule for your entire project, set `enabled: false` in your `.flak.yml`.

```yaml
# .flak.yml
rules:
  line-length:
    enabled: false
```

### Inline Comments

You can disable rules for specific lines using inline comments. This is useful for one-off exceptions.

ignore:
  - 'node_modules/'
  - 'vendor/'

# ❄️ flak

**A fast, simple, and opinionated linter for your YAML files.**

`flak` helps you catch common mistakes, enforce best practices, and maintain a consistent style in your YAML configuration, from CI/CD pipelines to Kubernetes manifests.

[![PyPI version](https://badge.fury.io/py/flak-linter.svg)](https://badge.fury.io/py/flak-linter)
[![Build Status](https://github.com/your-username/flak/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/your-username/flak/actions/workflows/ci.yml)
[![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-yellow.svg)](https://opensource.org/licenses/MIT)

---

## Table of Contents

- [Why `flak`?](#why-flak)
- [Features](#features)
- [Installation](#installation)
- [Usage](#usage)
- [Configuration](#configuration)
  - [Example `.flak.yml`](#example-flakyml)
- [Example Workflow](#example-workflow)
- [Available Rules](#available-rules)
- [Disabling Rules](#disabling-rules)
  - [In Configuration File](#in-configuration-file)
  - [Inline Comments](#inline-comments)
- [Contributing](#contributing)
- [License](#license)

## Why `flak`?

YAML is designed to be human-readable, but it's notoriously strict and prone to subtle errors that can be hard to spot. A misplaced indent, a trailing space, or an unquoted boolean can break your application or deployment.

`flak` is designed to be:
- **Fast:** Get feedback in milliseconds, perfect for pre-commit hooks and CI pipelines.
- **Simple:** Zero-config by default. Just run it on your files.
- **Helpful:** Error messages are clear, pointing directly to the line and column with a suggestion for a fix.
- **Fixable:** Includes a `--fix` option to automatically correct many common issues.

## Features

- ✅ **Syntax and Style Checking:** Catches everything from duplicate keys to inconsistent indentation.
- ⚙️ **Customizable:** Configure rules, exclude files, and set standards in a `.flak.yml` file.
- 🪄 **Auto-fixing:** Use `flak --fix` to automatically correct simple style violations.
- 🚀 **CI/CD Friendly:** Exits with a non-zero status code when issues are found, integrating seamlessly into your workflows.
- 🔌 **Extensible:** (Future) Support for custom plugins and rules.

## Installation

The recommended way to install `flak` is with `pipx` to ensure it's in an isolated environment.

```bash
pipx install flak-linter
```

Alternatively, you can use `pip`:

```bash
pip install flak-linter
```

*(Note: The package name on PyPI is `flak-linter` to avoid name conflicts.)*

## Usage

Lint a single file:
```bash
flak config/production.yml
```

Lint multiple files or use a glob pattern:
```bash
flak k8s/*.yaml services/**/*.yml
```

Lint an entire directory recursively:
```bash
flak .
```

Automatically fix correctable errors:
```bash
flak --fix .
```

View all available options:
```bash
flak --help
```

## Configuration

For project-specific settings, create a `.flak.yml` file in your project's root directory. `flak` will automatically discover and use it.

### Example `.flak.yml`

```yaml
# .flak.yml

# Files and directories to ignore. Supports glob patterns.
exclude:
  - 'node_modules/'
  - 'vendor/'
  - '**/chart/templates/*.yaml'

# Override default rule settings.
rules:
  # Enforce 2-space indentation.
  indentation:
    level: 2
    check-multi-line-strings: true

  # Disable the key-quotes rule entirely.
  key-quotes:
    enabled: false

  # Set the max line length to 120 characters.
  line-length:
    max: 120
```

## Example Workflow

Let's say you have a file `deployment.yml` with a few issues:

```yaml
# deployment.yml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: my-app  
spec:
    replicas: "3" # Booleans and numbers shouldn't be quoted
  template:
    # ...
```

Running `flak` on it will produce clear, actionable output:

```bash
$ flak deployment.yml

✖ Found 2 issues in deployment.yml
  deployment.yml:4:15   error     Trailing whitespace detected. (trailing-whitespace)
  deployment.yml:6:15   warning   Numeric value should not be quoted. (quoted-numerics)

Run `flak --fix` to attempt to automatically fix 2 issues.
```

Now, run the auto-fixer:

```bash
$ flak --fix deployment.yml
✓ Fixed 2 issues in deployment.yml
```

The file is now clean:

```yaml
# deployment.yml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: my-app
spec:
  replicas: 3 # Booleans and numbers shouldn't be quoted
  template:
    # ...
```

## Available Rules

Here is a list of core rules available in `flak`.

| Rule ID               | Description                                        | Auto-fixable |
| --------------------- | -------------------------------------------------- | :----------: |
| `indentation`         | Enforces consistent indentation (default: 2 spaces). |      ✅      |
| `trailing-whitespace` | Disallows trailing whitespace on lines.            |      ✅      |
| `key-duplicates`      | Disallows duplicate keys within the same mapping.  |      ❌      |
| `quoted-booleans`     | Enforces booleans (`true`/`false`) are not quoted. |      ✅      |
| `quoted-numerics`     | Enforces numeric values are not quoted.            |      ✅      |
| `hyphen-spacing`      | Enforces a single space after a list item hyphen.  |      ✅      |
| `line-length`         | Checks for lines exceeding a maximum length.       |      ❌      |
| `empty-lines`         | Limits the number of consecutive empty lines.      |      ✅      |

## Disabling Rules

### In Configuration File

To disable a rule for your entire project, set `enabled: false` in your `.flak.yml`.

```yaml
# .flak.yml
rules:
  line-length:
    enabled: false
```

### Inline Comments

You can disable rules for specific lines using inline comments. This is useful for one-off exceptions.

- **Disable for a single line:**
  ```yaml
  long_line: "this is an exceptionally long line that we have to make an exception for" # flak:disable-line line-length
  ```

- **Disable for the next line:**
  ```yaml
  # flak:disable-next-line key-quotes
  "key-with-special-chars-@": "value"
  ```

Contributions are welcome! If you'd like to add a new rule, fix a bug, or improve the documentation, please check out our [Contributing Guide](CONTRIBUTING.md) and the [Code of Conduct](CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md).

## 🎯 Why Flak?

YAML is designed to be human-readable, but its flexibility can lead to inconsistencies and subtle errors that are hard to spot.

-   **Indentation matters:** A single misplaced space can break everything.
-   **Inconsistent styles:** Are booleans `true`/`false` or `yes`/`no`? Are strings quoted or not?
-   **Common pitfalls:** Duplicate keys, trailing whitespace, or missing document separators.

`flak` automates the process of checking for these issues, so you can focus on what the configuration *does*, not how it's formatted.

## ✨ Features

-   **🚀 Fast:** Built to be performant, linting large codebases in seconds.
-   **🔧 Configurable:** Define your own ruleset in a `.flak.yaml` file.
-   **🤖 CI/CD Friendly:** Exits with a non-zero status code on failure, making it perfect for automation.
-   **✍️ Auto-fix Support:** Automatically fix simple style violations with the `--fix` flag.
-   **🔍 Glob Support:** Easily lint multiple files across your entire project.
-   **📚 Sensible Defaults:** Comes with a `recommended` ruleset out-of-the-box.

## 📦 Installation

You can install `flak` using pip:

```bash
pip install flak-linter
```

Alternatively, you can grab a pre-compiled binary from the [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/your-user/flak/releases) page.

## Usage

Using `flak` is straightforward. Pass it file paths or glob patterns.

### Basic Linting

```bash
# Lint a single file
flak config.yaml

# Lint multiple files
flak service/deployment.yaml service/configmap.yaml

# Lint all YAML files in a directory (recursively)
flak 'kubernetes/**/*.yaml'

# Lint the entire current directory
flak .
```

### Auto-fixing Issues

For rules that support it, `flak` can automatically fix violations.

```bash
flak --fix my-messy-file.yaml
```

### Getting Help

```bash
flak --help
```

### Exit Codes

-   `0`: Success! No linting errors were found.
-   `1`: An error occurred (e.g., invalid arguments).
-   `2`: Linting errors were found.

This makes `flak` ideal for use in Git hooks or CI/CD pipelines.

## ⚙️ Configuration

To configure `flak`, create a `.flak.yaml` or `.flak.yml` file in your project's root directory.

### Example `.flak.yaml`

```yaml
# Start with the recommended ruleset
extends: recommended

# Ignore specific files or directories
ignore:
  - 'vendor/**'
  - 'node_modules/**'
  - 'ci/generated-*.yaml'

# Customize or override rules
rules:
  # Rule: level, [options]
  # Levels: 'error', 'warn', 'off'

  # Enforce 2-space indentation instead of the default
  indentation: [error, 2]

  # Warn about unquoted keys instead of erroring
  key-quotes: warn

  # Allow "yes"/"no" for booleans (not recommended)
  truthy-values: off

  # Require --- at the start of a document
  document-start: error

  # Disallow duplicate keys in mappings
  key-duplicates: error
```

### Rules

`flak` supports a variety of rules. Here are a few common ones:

| Rule              | Description                                        | Fixable |
| ----------------- | -------------------------------------------------- | :-----: |
| `indentation`     | Enforces a consistent indentation width (e.g., 2). |   ✅    |
| `trailing-spaces` | Disallows trailing whitespace on lines.            |   ✅    |
| `key-duplicates`  | Prevents duplicate keys within the same mapping.   |   ❌    |
| `truthy-values`   | Requires boolean values to be `true` or `false`.   |   ✅    |
| `document-start`  | Requires documents to start with `---`.            |   ✅    |
| `colons`          | Enforces consistent spacing around colons.         |   ✅    |
| `empty-lines`     | Manages the number of empty lines.                 |   ✅    |

You can easily add `flak` to your CI pipeline to enforce YAML quality.

name: Lint YAML

on:

    branches: [ main ]

      - name: Set up Python

        with:
          python-version: '3.11'

      - name: Install flak
        run: pip install flak-linter

      - name: Run flak

This workflow will automatically check all YAML files on every push and pull request to the `main` branch.

# flak ⚡️

A blazingly fast, configurable linter for your YAML files.

[![Build Status](https://img.shields.io/github/actions/workflow/status/your-username/flak/ci.yml?branch=main&style=for-the-badge)](https://github.com/your-username/flak/actions)
[![PyPI version](https://img.shields.io/pypi/v/flak-linter?style=for-the-badge)](https://pypi.org/project/flak-linter/)
[![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-yellow.svg?style=for-the-badge)](https://opensource.org/licenses/MIT)

---

`flak` helps you enforce consistent styles, catch common errors, and maintain high-quality YAML files across your projects. Whether you're managing Kubernetes manifests, GitHub Actions workflows, or application configurations, `flak` ensures your YAML is clean, correct, and readable.

 <!-- It's highly recommended to replace this with an actual screenshot or asciinema recording of your tool in action -->

## Features

-   **⚡️ Blazingly Fast:** Built with performance in mind to lint large codebases in seconds.
-   **🛠️ Highly Configurable:** Use a `.flak.yml` file to customize rules, exclude files, and share configurations.
-   **🤖 Autofix Support:** Automatically fix many common issues with the `--fix` flag.
-   **✅ Comprehensive Ruleset:** Comes with a wide range of built-in rules for formatting, syntax, and best practices.
-   **🔌 CI/CD Friendly:** Integrates easily into your CI pipelines with non-zero exit codes and various output formats.
-   **🤫 Inline Disabling:** Easily disable rules for a specific line or block using comments.

## Installation

You can install `flak` using pip:

```bash
pip install flak-linter
```

*(Note: The package name is `flak-linter` to avoid conflicts on PyPI, but the command remains `flak`.)*

Alternatively, you can use `pipx` for a clean, isolated installation:

```bash
pipx install flak-linter
```

## Usage

### Basic Linting

Lint one or more files or directories. `flak` will automatically discover `.yml` and `.yaml` files.

```bash
# Lint a single file
flak config/production.yml

# Lint multiple files
flak docker-compose.yml .github/workflows/ci.yml

# Lint all YAML files in a directory recursively
flak kubernetes/
```

### Linting from stdin

You can also pipe content directly to `flak`. Use `-` as the filename to indicate stdin.

```bash
cat my-config.yml | flak -
```

### Autofixing Errors

For rules that support it, `flak` can automatically fix errors.

```bash
flak --fix .
```

## Configuration

`flak` can be configured by placing a `.flak.yml` file in your project's root directory.

Here is an example `.flak.yml` file:

```yaml
# .flak.yml

# You can extend a shared configuration
extends: ./.github/flak-base.yml

# Specify files and directories to ignore
exclude:
  - 'node_modules/'
  - 'vendor/'
  - '**/legacy-config.yml'

# Configure specific rules. Set a rule to `false` to disable it.
rules:
  # Enforce 2-space indentation
  indentation: 2

  # Disallow trailing spaces
  trailing-spaces: true

  # Enforce specific casing for keys (camelCase, snake_case, or kebab-case)
  key-casing: 'snake_case'

  # Disable the key-ordering rule
  key-ordering: false
```

`flak` will automatically search for a `.flak.yml` file in the current directory and its parent directories.

## Available Rules

`flak` comes with a set of built-in rules. Here are some of the most common ones:

| Rule ID           | Description                                                 | Autofixable |
| ----------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- | ----------- |
| `indentation`     | Enforces a consistent indentation width (e.g., 2 or 4).     | ✅          |
| `key-duplicates`  | Disallows duplicate keys within the same mapping.           | ❌          |
| `key-ordering`    | Enforces alphabetical ordering of keys in mappings.         | ✅          |
| `trailing-spaces` | Disallows whitespace at the end of lines.                   | ✅          |
| `empty-lines`     | Prevents more than a specified number of consecutive empty lines. | ✅          |
| `truthy-values`   | Enforces the use of `true`/`false` over `yes`/`no`/`on`/`off`. | ✅          |
| `hyphens`         | Enforces consistent spacing for sequence hyphens.           | ✅          |
| `colons`          | Enforces consistent spacing after colons in mappings.       | ✅          |
| `quotes`          | Enforces a consistent quote style (`single` or `double`).   | ✅          |

*For a full list of rules and their configuration options, please see the official documentation (link to docs here).*

## Ignoring Errors

You can disable `flak` for a specific line by adding a comment.

```yaml
# Disable all rules for the next line
key: value  # flak:ignore

# Disable a specific rule for the next line
service:
  name: my-app  # flak:ignore key-ordering
  image: my-image
```

To disable multiple rules, separate them with a comma:

```yaml
# flak:ignore key-ordering, indentation
misaligned:
  b_key: 2
  a_key: 1
```

Contributions are welcome! We are always looking for improvements to the core linter, new rules, and better documentation.

Please read our [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) for details on our code of conduct and the process for submitting pull requests.

cargo install flak-linter

flak config.yaml
